# delulu-smash

> *The simplicity & efficiency of Omarchy, the exploration of Jupyter, the composability of VS Code, and the
> extensibility & flexibility of Pi: your desktop hub.*
>
> The design rules that follow from this: `spec/services/ui/README.md` ("The spirit of the app").

A browser workbench built with [Reflex](https://reflex.dev), in the spirit of
`experimental/textual-kernel`: chat with the Smash agent (`ds.ai.agent`) across the top; below
it, everything its tools return shows up as a tab named `r1`, `r2`, … (tables as sortable, filterable
grids, VODs (match videos) as a playable gallery, other results as a field list), side by side with
Jupyter-style Python cells where those names are plain Python objects (tables are polars DataFrames).
Drag the chat strip's or the tables pane's bottom-right corner to resize them. The bottom bar shows or hides each pane.

```sh
cd services/ui
uv run reflex run
# -> http://localhost:3000
```

Design intent lives in `spec/services/ui/`: navigation, keys and much of the look follow
Omarchy (`spec/services/ui/omarchy.md`).

## Desktop app

On Omarchy this app is **delulu-smash**: `SUPER+SHIFT+I` opens it in its own web app window, or focuses
the one already open (`.os/scripts/keybindings/delulu-smash.sh`). The server runs as a systemd user
service, `~/.config/systemd/user/delulu-smash.service`, started at login by `~/.config/hypr/autostart.lua`;
if it isn't up, the shortcut starts it and opens the window once it answers (cold start up to about
a minute). It's also in the app launcher as the delulu-smash web app. All of this is tracked by `os sync`.

```sh
ds ui restart                              # eg after changing dependencies (`ds settings sync` runs it itself)
ds ui status                               # up / down
journalctl --user -u delulu-smash -f       # server logs
```

The service runs `ds ui run` (`reflex run` in dev mode), so code edits hot-reload in the open window. Stop it
before running the app by hand (both use ports 3000 and 8000).

Runs from the repo's root venv (no own `pyproject.toml`); needs the AI Gateway key the rest of
`ds.ai` uses.

- **Chat**: Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line. ArrowUp in the empty box brings back the last message you
  sent (slash commands and `@` prints too), again for the one before; ArrowDown goes forward, and past the
  newest back to the empty box, as in a terminal. It only works while the box is empty or still shows a
  recalled message untouched: edit it and the arrows move the cursor again. Kept in this browser
  (`assets/history.js`: localStorage, the newest 100, a message sent twice in a row once). Tool calls are listed above each reply. While the agent works,
  light sweeps across the chat box (as over the code in an inline chat).
  Scroll up and a round ↓ button appears over the bottom of the chat: it jumps back to the newest message.
  Hover a message for its copy button on the top-right corner (a reply copies as its markdown source).
  A code block in a reply is the app's own dark block (`ui.markdown_code`, `.md-code`: as the help panel's
  snippets, not `rx.markdown`'s light highlighter; plain text, no syntax colours), with its own copy button
  on hover that copies the code alone.
  A failed turn (the model or a tool raised) shows its traceback in the same component a Python cell uses
  (`render.traceback_view`): the frame that raised and the error, the rest folded, and a copy button (top right,
  on hover) that copies the full plain-text traceback.
  Each tool result gets a row (`r1 · tool · 10 VODs`): click it to unfold the result inline (grid,
  gallery, fields; folded by default), or `open →` to open it as a tab in Results.
  Under each answer, a dim line says what the turn used (`$0.0011 · 21.3k in (71% cached) · 812 out · 3 requests`),
  summed from each model request's usage (`session.TurnUsage`); its `3 requests` is a link that opens the debug log on its
  Requests tab. The cost is what the Pydantic AI Gateway reported
  (pydantic-ai falls back to its bundled genai-prices data; `$?` when neither knows). Input counts each request's
  whole prompt, so a turn with tool calls counts the history once per request.
  The window's title bar (beside the app's mark at its left: the GitHub profile picture as a 22 px circle, `assets/avatar.png`; so it shows whichever panels are open) has a context
  meter, eg `context 4% · this session $0.0001` (hovering it shows the tokens in place of the percent, eg `43k / 1M tokens`): the conversation's size (the last request's input + output, what the next
  turn sends again) against the model's context window (from pydantic-ai's model profile), as tokens and a whole
  percent, and what the AI cost so far (chat turns and inline chats). It turns yellow past half full: answers there are slower and dearer, and a new chat starts small.
  Both are always there: the context meter starts at `context 0% · this session $0`,
  and next to it this month's spend: `month $-- / $-- (--%)` and `as of --` until read, then eg `month $1.91 / $15 (13%)` (or
  `· no limit` / `· limit unknown`, the tooltip says why; colours as the Spend tab's). Monthly only (see the
  Spend tab below),
  in a thin box ending with when they were read, eg `as of 11/17 15:42`: they aren't live. Read once when the app
  opens (1 Logfire query, its project info, 3 limit lookups) and again on the Spend tab's Refresh;
  a click opens that tab. A failed read keeps the last numbers and says so in the tooltip.
- **Debug log** (bug icon in the title bar, `Alt+D`): every outside call the app made, newest first:
  start.gg GraphQL requests (operation, page, status, time, start.gg's object count), other HTTP fetches
  (supermajor search, smash-tube), agent turns (time, tool calls, tokens, cost; a `model requests` section lists each model request's tokens, cost, why it stopped and the tools it called) and tool steps (a tool step has a `tool response` section, folded
  until clicked: what the tool gave back to the AI, cut at 4,000 characters). A row unfolds to its
  details: the request as sent (method, url, headers with secrets filtered, body or GraphQL query and
  variables), the response (status, type, size, `cf-ray`, the start of an error body), page info, timing
  (including the wait for start.gg's rate budget), the lookup's `group`, session, origin
  (`chat` / `form` / `view` / `cell`) and error. Copy buttons give the record as JSON and the request as a curl
  command (secrets as `$AUTHORIZATION` / `$APIKEY`, set them before running it). A row's `↖` link goes to
  where it came from, with the same scroll-and-flash as Show in Chat (`State.reveal`, `window.reveal` in
  `assets/panes.js`, the app's one way of navigating): the tool call's row in the chat (records made during a
  tool call carry its `tool_call_id`, from `ds.ai.call_log.ToolCallLog`), the chat turn, the result tab whose
  form ran it, or the cell. The other way round, the bug on a tool call or your message in the chat, or on a
  cell (on hover), or Show Requests in a result tab's right-click menu, opens the log on just that thing's
  requests (`State.show_logs`, `logs.in_focus`; the same target ids as the links). On top:
  start.gg requests in the last 60 s against the 80 allowed, the backend's memory, and this session's variables
  (count, rough size). It opens on **this session's** records only (so a fresh window's log is empty): the
  backend is a long-running service and keeps one log for every window, so untick "this session only" to see the
  other windows' records too (and those made outside any browser tab). Filter by kind; Clear forgets what is shown
  (this session's, or everything when unticked). Records come from
  `ds.util.http` / `ds.util.graphql` and are kept in memory only (`ui/logs.py`, newest 2000, gone on restart);
  the panel loads them when opened, on Refresh and when a turn, form or cell finishes, never while closed.
  A new kind of record is one function in `logs.LOG_FORMATS`.
  The panel goes full screen with the arrows at its top right, or `Alt+F` while it is open (Esc goes back to
  the side panel first, then closes it); it reopens the way you left it.
  Four tabs: **Requests** (the log above), **System**, **Spend** and **Agents**:
  - **System** (`ui/perf.py`): where the memory is and what was slow, to understand the app while
    using it. Read when you click the tab and on its Refresh, never in the background; nothing is stored
    beyond the timings below.
    - **Tiles**: the backend's memory now and at its peak, the sessions it holds, handlers that took over
      300 ms, CPU used, time since the backend started (a code edit in dev mode restarts it).
    - **Memory**: the parts that can be measured, as bars on one scale (the backend's total): this session's
      variables, its SmashDb (loaded once per session), its chat, the other sessions, the debug log, the
      timings. "Everything else" is the rest: Python, polars, Reflex and the libraries. Sizes are rough (a
      DataFrame's buffers, a model's JSON): for spotting what is big, not accounting.
    - **Biggest variables**: this session's Python names by size, with type and shape.
    - **Sessions**: every browser tab that ever opened the app, with when it opened, when it was last used,
      what it holds and what its AI cost. A session is never dropped: a closed window keeps its variables
      until the backend restarts, and this table is where that shows.
    - **Handlers and steps**: every event handler of the app is timed, from the event arriving to its last
      update (`state.event`, which is `rx.event` plus `perf.timed`): runs, median, p95, max, total, sorted by
      total. `view_event` is split by action (`view_event: sort`); rows named `step:` are parts of a handler
      (`build view`: a value made into what the browser gets; `sync tabs`: every variable re-read into the
      tab list). A handler that waits on a fetch counts the wait. Orange = p95 over 300 ms.
    - **Slowest runs**: the single slowest runs, with when and whose session.
    - **Outside calls**: the Requests tab's records summed by what was called (start.gg operation, site,
      agent, tool): runs, median, max, total, errors.
    - **State held for this tab**: the Reflex state's vars by size as JSON, ie what the server keeps and
      sends for this window (a 2000-row grid in `view` shows here).
    - **Browser**: measured by the page itself (`window.perfSnapshot`, `assets/panes.js`): JS heap, DOM nodes,
      long tasks (the page frozen for over 50 ms) since load, page load time, mounted editors.
    - **Process**: pid, threads, open files, polars' thread pool, tracked Python objects, versions.
    - **Copy report** gives all of it as plain text, eg to paste into a chat with an AI. **Clear timings**
      forgets the kept timings, to measure from now.
    - Timings are kept in memory only (the newest 5000, every session, about 100 bytes each; gone on restart),
      like the log's records. A new timed step is `with perf.span("name"):`; a new handler is timed by using
      `@event` (background handlers use plain `rx.event(background=True)` and are not timed).
  - **Spend** (`ui/spend.py`, `ds.data.raw.logfire`, `ds.data.raw.gateway`): AI spend from Logfire, so
    every machine and app that traces there (chat, inline chats, evals), not only this session, next to
    the Gateway's spending limits:
    - **This month** (UTC; the cap's window, assumed, the Gateway's docs don't say), against the tighter
      of the project's and the organization's monthly cap, written as the Gateway's own page does:
      `$1.44 of $15.00`, a meter (green, yellow from 75%, red from 90%), then `$13.56 remaining · 9% used`;
      `· No limit` when none is set, `· limit unknown` when they can't be read. One "Limits:" line names
      both levels' monthly caps. **Monthly only**: no today / this week figures or daily / weekly caps
      (the Gateway has them; they aren't read), since the traced daily figure didn't match the Gateway's
      billed one (haiku traces carry no cost) and the monthly cap is the one in use.
    - **Chart**: a bar per day (local days, last 30) on a $ scale with a y axis (top, half, 0): the
      history, not a limit.
    - A split by agent and model, the priciest requests (copy a trace id to find it in Logfire).
    - Asked only when you click the Spend tab or its Refresh (the panel always opens on Requests): Logfire's
      query API (three requests) and its management API for the limits (three more), each logged in the
      Requests tab; nothing stored.
    - Needs both Pydantic keys `ds settings sync` stores (it then restarts the app): the project key
      for the spend (the chat's key too), the organization key (with `organization:read_gateway`)
      for the limits; the Gateway refuses the organization key for model calls. Without the project key the tab says how to get it;
      without a working organization key it shows spend and says why the limits are missing. Only priced, traced calls count (a model the Gateway
      has no price for counts as $0, and the note says how many).
    The agents' info needs no request (read from the Agent objects; prices from genai-prices' bundled data).
  - **Agents** (`ui/agents.py`): each agent the app runs (`smash-agent` for the chat and `ds ai eval`,
    `inline-edit` for Alt+I in an editor, `inline-fill` for Alt+I in a widget's form) with its model, provider, context window, list price per 1M tokens (genai-prices),
    model settings, output type and retries, then what the model is actually given, named as pydantic-ai
    names it: the agent's `instructions` (its prompt), and each capability with whether it is deferred
    (`defer_loading=True`) or always-on, its `description`, its own `instructions` and its `tools` (each
    tool's description and parameters). A dashed `How it loads` box at the top of a card is the app's own
    explanation of that setup, marked as not being text the model gets. `Copy setup` copies one
    agent's whole setup as text. Read once from the Agent objects at start, so no request is made; the chat
    title shows the chat agent's model.
    - **Why a tool wasn't used**: the chat agent's capabilities are all deferred (`defer_loading=True`). A request starts with
      only the agent's instructions, the tool `load_capability` and a list of capability ids with their
      descriptions; a capability's tools and instructions don't exist for the model until it loads that
      capability, which it decides from the description alone. The card says so at its top, and each
      capability shows `loaded in this chat` or `not loaded in this chat`.
    - **This chat** (top of the tab): the capabilities this chat's model loaded and how often it called each
      tool, read from the chat's message history (`agents.activity`) when the tab opens and after a turn.
- **Tables**: click a tab to switch, type in the filter box to search. Click a column header to sort
  (ascending, descending, unsorted); filter and sort work the same in a tab and in a cell's result.
  The grid shows at most 2000 rows; the DataFrame itself is never truncated.
- **Widgets are data-driven** (`ui/widgets.py`): every kind of view is a row in `WIDGETS`, and the
  app reads a widget's behaviour from that row instead of hard-coding it per widget:

  | attribute | meaning |
  | --- | --- |
  | `kind`, `title` | the view kind `render.py` draws, and its name for people |
  | `tool`, `hide` | the agent tool it mimics: gives it a tool form (below) and the inline chat that fills it; `hide` = parameters not on the form |
  | `new` | for a widget that is no tool's result: the blank value `+` binds (eg a SmashDb console) |
  | `addable` | offered in the Results tab bar's `+` menu, to add by hand (needs `tool` or `new`) |
  | `chat_open` | starts unfolded in the chat when the agent returns it (others start as a folded row) |

  Today: `table`, `vods` (match videos, called VODs as the Smash community does; the agent's tool and its type keep their names, `find_match_videos` / `MatchVideos`; addable), `usage` (`get_player_usage`, addable, unfolded in
  chat), `fields`, `smashdb` (the SmashDb console, addable), `tool`. A new attribute is a field on `Widget` plus the one place that reads it. A new widget
  is a row, a `case` in `render.to_view`, and its component in `render.render_component`. Whether it gets the
  inline chat is asked each time one is added (with a `tool` it does by default; see
  `spec/services/ui/inline_ai.md`).
- **Links look like links, in every widget**: text that opens a url is drawn with `render.link(text, href)`:
  blue and underlined, exactly as a link in the agent's markdown reply (`.md a, a.link` in `assets/app.css`),
  opening in a new tab. Don't style a hyperlink as plain text, and don't give a widget its own link style.
  The one other form is a link drawn as a button (the video player's `YouTube ↗`, class `act`).
- **Player usage** (kind `usage`, `ds.data.startgg.PlayerUsage`, built from start.gg sets; it replaced the
  supermajor.gg version when that site began blocking automated clients): a player at a glance. Its form has
  `player`, `vs characters` (several picks; games against any of them count), `setting` and `sets` (how many of
  their newest sets it reads, 30 to 150; each 30 is one start.gg request). An All / Offline /
  Online toggle at the top picks which events the whole view counts; it runs the tool again with that
  `setting` (a few seconds the first time, since offline-only reaches further back than the capped mix), and
  each recent event carries an `offline` (filled) or `online` (outlined) tag and its name is a link to the
  event's start.gg page. Characters as ranked bars with
  their stock icons (switch between all games, game 1 and events), one line on how often they change
  character within a set, stages in three groups (starters, counterpicks, taken to; often empty, since many
  brackets report no stages), and the characters played at each recent event as icons (hover for games). The
  tab's note gives the real date span and the set / game counts. No results are shown. Past 6 rows the tail folds
  into one "N others" row; hover a row for the count. Bars rather than a pie: lengths on one baseline compare
  close shares exactly, and the icons, not colours, say which character. The icons are
  `pkgs/ds/data/char_icons/` (`ds.data.char_icon_by_name`), served by the backend (`api.py`).
- **Tool forms** (`ui/tool_forms.py`): some results show the inputs of the agent tool that made
  them. `Inputs ▸` in their bar folds them open, filled with what the tool was called with; change them and
  press Enter (or Run) to run the tool again in place. The `+` at the end of the Results tab bar (a small menu with a search box), or an
  `Add: ...` command in the command palette (`Alt+P`), adds one
  by hand: a placeholder (`ToolRequest`) that is just the form, replaced by the result on its first run.
  How the form stays aligned with the tool:
  - **Fields** are built from the tool's parameter schema, the one pydantic-ai gives the model
    (`schema_fields`: names, types, defaults, descriptions; a `Literal` becomes a dropdown). Nothing about a
    tool's parameters is written a second time.
  - **The type decides the input, not the name**, so any tool gets the same one:

    | type hint | input |
    | --- | --- |
    | `str` | text box |
    | `int` / `float` | number box |
    | `bool` | checkbox |
    | `Literal[...]` / `Enum` | dropdown |
    | `CharEnum` (eg `CharGroup`) | choice input, one pick |
    | `list[CharGroup]`, `list[Literal[...]]`, `list[SomeEnum]` | choice input, several picks |
    | `list[str]` | text box (no options to pick from) |

    Conventions:
    - The choice input is one component, single or multiple (`render._choice_input`, `assets/choice.js`,
      `tool_forms.picker_for`): a box with a chip per pick (× removes it) that opens the list. The only
      difference: several picks tick and untick with the list kept open; one pick replaces the last.
    - A long list (over `CHOICE_SEARCH_AT`, 8 options, eg characters) gets a search box on top, single or
      multiple alike; a short one (eg `rounds`) doesn't.
    - `T | None` gets the same input as `T` for dropdowns and choice inputs. A plain `int | None` /
      `bool | None` gets a text box (its schema is an `anyOf` with no single `type`).
    - The parameter's default fills the input, and its docstring description is the tooltip.
    - An empty input means the default (`any` for choice inputs).
    - A choice input submits `a,b`, which `tool_forms.arguments` turns back into `T`'s values.
    - To change an input, change the type hint. The form code needs no edit (`ToolForm.fields`;
      tested in `tests/services/ui/test_widgets.py`).
  - **Values** go through the validator pydantic-ai uses for the model's calls, then the same tool function.
  - **Which inputs made a result** is recorded by the session (`Session.calls`): the agent's tool-call
    arguments, or the form as run. Paging keeps them; a value made in Python has none (an empty form).
    The form shows what the tool was called with (eg `player_1=Joker`), the bar what was really searched.
  - **Back to the original**: for a result the agent made, the session also keeps the agent's own call
    (`Call.original`: its inputs and result). Once the form is re-run, `Inputs` turns green and an × in
    the form puts both back, without fetching again (`Session.restore_original`). A form added by hand
    has no original.
  - `tests/services/ui/test_tool_forms.py` checks every tool form; `test_widgets.py` the registry.

  Which widgets have one is `Widget.tool` in `widgets.py`; `_bar` adds the `Inputs` button to any view with
  a form, and the widget's component places `form_section` under its bar.
- **Table SQL** (as in DBeaver): `SQL ▸` in a table's bar unfolds a one-line SQL box under it, starting
  as `select * from self`. Ctrl+Enter (`Shortcut.RUN_SQL`) runs it on the table with polars' `df.sql`
  (PostgreSQL syntax, the table is `self`), and the grid shows the result, still filtered and sorted by
  the bar; `SQL` turns green while a query is applied, and × goes back to the whole table. A bad query
  shows its error and leaves the table as it was. The query is kept per view slot, like the filter
  (`Ui.sql`, `View.table`); the value bound to the name is never changed.
- **SmashDb console** (kind `smashdb`, `ui/db_console.py`; `+` → SmashDb console): a small
  DataGrip. Left, the schema tree: every table with its row count; click one to unfold its columns and
  dtypes, `▶` (on hover) selects everything from it. Right, the query editor (the table SQL box's CodeMirror,
  completing every table and column): Ctrl+Enter (`Shortcut.RUN_SQL`) or Run runs it; with text selected only
  the selection runs, so several queries can sit in the box. Under it the result, which is the table widget
  itself (`render._table_bar` / `_table_body`): the same grid, header sort, row filter and `SQL ▸` on `self`
  as any DataFrame; the bar's note adds the time the query took. A failed query keeps the last result and
  shows its traceback in the component a Python cell and the chat use (`render.traceback_view`). `History ▸`
  lists this console's queries that ran (newest first, 20, each once); click one to put it back in the editor.
  - It queries the session's `db`, the one the Python cells have, so `create table x as select ...` in the
    console is there in a cell and the other way round (in memory only; the parquet files are never written).
  - The tab's name is bound to the console: `r3.df` is the result DataFrame, `r3.sql` its query.
  - **Save as ▸** (in the bar, once a query has run) keeps the result under a name of your own: the next free
    `q1`, `q2`, ... is filled in, so Enter alone saves, or type one. It is bound in Python like `q1 = <result>`
    and gets its own tab; you stay in the console. It is the query's result, without the bar's row filter, sort
    or `SQL ▸`. A name that isn't a Python name, starts with `_`, is `pl` / `db` or is the console itself is
    refused; an existing name is replaced, as in Python.
  - Running a query makes a new `DbConsole` that replaces the old one at its slot, as a tool form's run does.
  - No cache: the tree is read from the db on every redraw (about 2 ms), so a new table shows at once.
- **Rendering** (`ui/render.py`): everything about showing a value lives in this one file, used
  for agent tool results, cell outputs and tabs alike. Today: DataFrame / Series / list of pydantic models
  -> grid; `MatchVideos` (the agent's `find_match_videos`, smash-tube.com) -> thumbnail gallery; any other
  pydantic model -> its fields, with lists of models as small tables; `DbConsole` -> the SmashDb console;
  everything else -> its repr.
  Every widget's bar ends with its float button (⤢, Alt+F) and a × (`render.close_view_button`), which
  closes it as fits where it is shown (`State._close_view`): a Results tab closes, a glance closes (the
  layout goes back), a chat row folds (the row stays), a cell's output is hidden.
  It is two matches, because Reflex compiles components ahead of time and the browser never sees the
  Python object: `to_view(value)` is a Python `match` on the value's type (run when a cell or tool
  returns), and `render_component(view)` picks the component for the view's kind. To add a type, add a
  `case` to `to_view`; a new kind of view also needs a `case` (and its component) in `render_component`.
  **Design rule: a value renders as one contained component, the same wherever it is placed** (a tab,
  a cell output, later a popup or anything else). Everything that belongs to the view is inside what
  `render_component` returns: a table's filter and sort, a video list's player and paging. Its state
  (filter text, sort, picked video, folded list) travels in its `ViewData`, and the session keeps it
  per *slot*, the place a view is shown (`tab:<name>`, `chat:<name>` for a result unfolded in the chat, `cell:<id>`), so a view is back as it was left.
  Every interaction comes back through one handler, `State.view_event(slot, action, arg)`. A host only
  does `render_component(view, State.view_event)`: it adds nothing of the view's own around it, and
  `compact=True` changes sizing only. To show a view somewhere new, give that place a slot prefix
  (`Session.view_at` / `put`, `State._show`) and call `render_component`; no component logic is repeated.
- **Result tabs**: the x on a tab (or right-click: Close, Close Others, Close to the Right, Close All, as
  in VS Code) closes it. Only the tab goes: the name stays in Python, and the tab comes back when the name is
  bound to something new or the result is opened again from the chat (`Session.closed` / `tabs()`).
  A result the agent returned has `↖ chat` in its bar (and Show in Chat in the right-click menu): it
  scrolls the chat to that tool call's row and flashes it.
- **Help**: the ? at the top right (Alt+H), kept short: first **Panels** (`ui.PANELS`: each panel with the key
  that shows or hides it and its full-screen key, then the palette for everything else), then examples of slash commands and `@` mentions as code
  snippets (`HELP_EXAMPLES` in `ui.py`: what to type and what it does, coloured as in the chat box),
  the keyboard shortcuts in a box that scrolls (a few rows at a time; `Alt+K` is the searchable list), and an
  FAQ of fixes for common errors (`FAQ`: question, answer, commands to run). It is as tall as the window
  allows, then scrolls. How the app works lives here in the README, not in the panel.
- **App guide: the chat can explain the app** (`ui/app_guide.py`, `guide.md`): ask the chat how to use
  something, eg "show me how to use the script slash command" or "what key opens Python?". The chat agent
  gets a deferred capability, `app_guide`, with no tools: until an app question comes up the model sees one
  line; `load_capability` then brings in the whole of `services/ui/guide.md` (the words, written for the
  user: what to type and what shows; under 160 lines), plus every slash command and every key, added from
  `commands.SLASH` and `Shortcut` so those lists can't go stale. About 3k tokens, in that chat from then
  on (cached), and one extra model request for the load.
  - The guide is read from disk on each load (no cache), minus its HTML comments: an edit applies to the
    next chat that loads it. A missing file leaves the two lists and says so.
  - The model is told to answer app questions from the guide only and to say when it doesn't cover
    something. It can't run a slash command or press a key: it shows what to type.
  - The app adds it on each chat run (`Session.ask(capabilities=...)`), so `pkgs/ds/ai` and `ds ai eval`
    are unchanged; the debug panel's Agents tab lists it with the agent's own capabilities and says so
    (its instructions there are as read when the app started). The inline AIs and `/assign` don't have it.
  - **A new user-visible feature gets its lines in `guide.md`**; a slash command without any fails
    `tests/services/ui/test_app_guide.py`. The help panel (`Alt+H`) keeps its own examples.
- **Command palette** (`Alt+P`, `Shortcut.PALETTE`; as VS Code's Ctrl+Shift+P and Omarchy's menu): a search
  box over every action of the app, one row each: icon, `Group: name`, its shortcut. Type to filter (a
  group name or other words work too, eg `view`, `jupyter`), arrows move, Enter runs, Esc or `Alt+P` closes. It always opens on top, as Omarchy's launcher does
  (over the debug log, help, the keybindings list, a floating view), and closing it leaves those open.
  - Commands are data, in `ui/commands.py` (`COMMANDS`): `Add:` the widgets you can add by hand,
    `View:` show / hide Chat, Results, the Python console (the name says which: "Hide" when it is showing)
    and full screen, `Python:` new cell / run all / clear outputs, `Results:` close all tabs, `AI:` the two
    inline chats, `App:` keybindings, help, debug log. A new command is one row there.
  - `Go to: r1` rows list the open results: the palette is also a tab switcher.
  - The first rows are fixed (`commands.PALETTE_FIRST`): Help, then Chat, Python, Terminal, Results, Variables.
    After them come the commands you ran last, marked "recent" (the last 5, remembered in this browser's
    localStorage by `assets/panes.js`), then the rest as written.
  - A command that acts where you are (full screen, inline chat) uses where you were before the palette
    opened: the result or pane, or the editor you were last in.
- **Slash commands** (`Command.slash` in `ui/commands.py`, `assets/slash.js`): a palette command
  with a `slash` name can also be typed in the chat box, eg `/clear-chat`, and runs exactly what its palette
  row runs. Typing `/` lists them over the box: type to filter, Up / Down, Tab completes the name, Enter
  runs, Esc closes the list. A message starting with `/` is never sent to the agent (`State.submit_chat`):
  an unknown name gets a line saying which commands exist. A command that ran shows in the chat as a tool
  call does: a row with the command, the text after it and what it did (`▸ /clear-variables  cleared 3
  variables`, `▸ /python  Python console: shown`), and a widget it added unfolded under that row, as a
  tool's result is (`State.slash_ran`, chat kind `slash`). These rows are the app's: the agent never gets them.
  A new slash command is the `slash=` field on its row. The list starts with the most used ones
  (`commands.SLASH_FIRST`: the two clears), then the rest as written. A slash command is coloured where
  you type it (blue if it exists, orange if not; hovering the box says what it does, the same line the list
  shows beside it) and in the chat line of what ran. A textarea can't colour part of its text, so
  `assets/slash.js` draws the box's text again in a layer under it while it starts with `/`. Today:
  - `/clear-chat` (`Chat: Clear`): a new conversation. The chat's rows and what the agent remembers go; the
    variables it made (`r1`, ...) and the spend so far stay. Not undoable, and not while a turn is running.
  - `/clear-variables` (`Variables: Clear all`): every listed variable at once (as ticking them all and
    `Clear` in the Variables panel), with its 3 s Undo.
  - `/results`, `/python`, `/variables` (show or hide the pane), `/new-cell`, `/close-tabs`, `/help`,
    `/keys`, `/debug`.
  - **A widget is its kind**: `/vods`, `/usage`, `/smashdb` add it and show it in the chat, under the
    command, where it works as it does in a tab (`open →` on its row brings up the tab; the `+` menu and
    the palette still add it as a tab only).
  - **Text after a command** (`Command.takes`, `Command.slash_event`): a widget with a tool takes text, eg
    `/vods mkleo vs sparg0 grand finals` or `/usage tweek last 50 sets`. The widget is added and the text
    goes to the inline AI that fills its inputs (`State.add_widget_ask`, the same call as the form's
    `Ask AI` row), so the form in the chat opens with a proposal that you run: the AI never runs the tool
    (`spec/services/ui/inline_ai.md`). In the list such a command shows as `/vods <text>`
    and Tab completes it with a space, ready for the text. A command that takes no text is not run when
    text follows it, so `/clear-chat please don't` clears nothing.
- **Mentions** (`@name`; **experimental**, `ui/mentions.py`, `assets/mentions.js`; what must hold is
  in `spec/services/ui/variables.md`, "Mentions"): `@q1` in a chat box points at a variable, so
  the AI is told what it holds. Without it the agent only knows the results it made itself in this chat, not a
  console's `q1`, a cell's names or a form you ran again.
  - **Typing `@`** lists the variables at the box (name, type, shape, where it came from): type to filter,
    Up / Down, Tab or Enter completes, Esc closes. A name that isn't a variable (`@someone`, an email) is
    plain text.
    With no variables yet, a bare `@` still opens the list with one small line, "No variables";
    it goes as you type on, and Enter / Tab are the box's own then.
  - **After a name, `.` lists what can follow, as the Python console does** (`mentions.complete`, asked from
    the backend on each keystroke: `POST /mention_complete`): first its columns (`@q1.char`), a model's fields
    or a console's `df` and `sql` (`@r3.df`), then its attributes (`@q1.shape`, `@q1.columns`), then the
    methods a mention may call (`head()`, green). A kind icon on the left, the type on the right. Any depth
    (`@r3.df.`). Picking a method puts the cursor between its brackets. Only what a mention can use is listed.
  - **One method call, at the end** (`mentions.CALLS`): `@big.describe()`, `@q1.head(5)`,
    `@sets.char.value_counts()`, `@q1.sort("wins", descending=True)`,
    `@big.sql("select char, count(*) n from self group by 1")`. So you pick what the AI sees of a big table
    (also where the AI has no tools: a form's Ask AI row, `Alt+I`). The rules:
    - Only read-only methods on the list. A table (DataFrame): `head`, `tail`, `sample`, `slice`, `describe`,
      `sort`, `unique`, `drop_nulls`, `null_count`, `top_k`, `bottom_k`, `sum`, `mean`, `median`, `min`, `max`,
      `select`, `drop`, `sql`. A column (Series): the same without the last three, plus `value_counts`,
      `to_list`, `n_unique`. A new one is a name in `CALLS`.
    - Arguments are plain values (text, numbers, `True` / `False`, lists of those); they are read, never
      evaluated. `@q1.filter(pl.col("wins") > 3)` is refused: use `.sql("select * from self where wins > 3")`.
    - One call, last: `@q1.head(5).tail(1)` is refused (use `.sql(...)`, or `/assign`).
    - A call that is refused or fails sends nothing: a `not sent` row says why (and which methods exist), and
      the message is put back in the box to fix.
    - `@` never makes a variable on its own: `@q1.describe()` alone prints the result (`↗ tab` on it, or
      `/assign`, is how it gets a name).
    - Brackets after a variable or a column are not a call: `@q1 (the saved one)` is `@q1`.
  - **Where**: the chat box, a tool form's Ask AI row (so `/usage the top player in @q1` too) and the inline
    chat in a cell or SQL box.
  - **Colour**: a mention is purple (its whole path, a call through its closing bracket) where a slash command
    is blue, in the chat box as you type, in the message once sent, and in the
    chat's `@q1 ...` row under your message. (The two single-line boxes list and complete, without colour.)
    That row is a fold when there is text to show: `▸` opens what the AI was given for the mentions (the same
    text is in the debug log, on the turn's record, as `added to the prompt`).
  - **`@q1` alone prints it, as the Python console would** (the same text without the `@`, run in a cell), with
    no AI call. A variable unfolds in the chat as a result does. A part or a call's result
    (`@q1.char`, `@q1.describe()`) shows as a cell's result: the same grid, with `↗ tab` to keep it as
    `out<n>`. A value with no view (a number, text, a list) shows as its repr. The agent never gets these
    rows. Only the output is the console's: what may be called is still the list below.
  - **What the AI gets** (`mentions.describe`): added to the end of your message, as text. A table of at most
    50 rows and 4,000 characters goes whole, as CSV. A bigger one goes as its shape, columns and first 5 rows,
    and says it isn't all there. VODs / player usage go as JSON, a console as its query and result, anything
    else as its repr (each cut at 4,000 characters, with a note).
  - **Big tables in the chat**: the chat agent gets a tool, `query_variable(name, sql)`, to run SQL on the
    variable, or on a mention with a call (the table is `self`); what it returns is a new `r<n>`, at most 200 rows. The app adds the tool on
    each run (`Session.ask(toolsets=...)`), so `pkgs/ds/ai` and `ds ai eval` are unchanged; the debug panel's
    Agents tab says so. The inline AIs have no tools: there a big table is only its summary.
  - **A snapshot**: the AI gets the value as it is when you send. The text stays in the chat history; no object
    is kept, so clearing a mentioned variable still frees it. Built again on every send (no cache).
  - Each mention costs input tokens on that turn and every later one, as any chat text does.
- **`/assign`** (`ui/assign.py`, `assets/assign.js`; what must hold is in
  `spec/services/ui/variables.md`, "/assign"): a new variable whose code the AI writes.
  - **Use**: `/assign top5 = the five best players in @q1`, or without a name (`/assign the date Ultimate came
    out`) and the AI picks one, by Python's naming conventions for its type (`assign.NAMING`):
    `release_date` for a date, `started_at` for a datetime, `is_offline` for a bool, a plural
    for a list (`player_tags`), `n_sets` for a count. A name you give is kept as it is. Under the command a box shows the code, eg
    `top5 = q1.sort("wins", descending=True)["player"].head(5).to_list()`. Change it if you like (also the
    name), then Enter (or Run) runs it; Esc (or Drop) runs nothing. Shift+Enter is a new line.
  - **Computed or known**: the AI computes from what the session has when it can (your variables, `db`); what
    it only knows, or the chat states, it writes as a literal (`release = datetime.date(2018, 12, 7)`). The
    line under the code says which: `computed from your data`, or `from the AI's knowledge or the chat: not
    checked`.
  - **What a variable may be**: a `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `date`, `datetime`, `time` or `timedelta`; a
    list of those (one kind); a record, as a frozen pydantic model (its class is defined by the code and kept
    in the session, eg `PlayerSummary`); several records, as a list of models of one class. A DataFrame (make
    models: `[Model(**row) for row in df.iter_rows(named=True)]`), a dict, `None`, a tuple, a set or a Series
    is refused, with why, and nothing is bound. Checked on the value the code made, so your
    own edits are held to it too.
  - **Running**: the code runs in a copy of your namespace, so a failure (its traceback shows under the box,
    which stays for a fix) or a refused value changes nothing, and helper names don't stay. Then the variable
    is bound (an existing name is replaced, and the row says so) and printed under the code, as `@name` prints
    one. Its source in the Variables pane is `/assign`. `BaseModel`, `datetime` and `from_url` are given to
    the code.
  - **From a web page** (`pkgs/ds/ai/extract.py`): give a URL, eg `/assign aapl_daily = daily closes for the
    past year from https://www.google.com/finance/quote/AAPL:NASDAQ`. The proposal defines a model class and
    ends with `aapl_daily = from_url(url, list[DailyClose], "daily closing prices for the past year")`; the
    line under it says `from a web page: filled by AI when run, not checked`. Change the class if you like
    (its fields are what gets filled), then Enter:
    - The page is downloaded and one AI call fills the class from its text (a few seconds, well under a
      cent). Tables, and values a site labels only by CSS class, keep their labels.
    - If the text doesn't hold it (data loaded by JavaScript), a browser agent opens the page in the system
      Chromium (headless, `/usr/bin/chromium`; pydantic-ai-harness `PlaywrightBrowser`, locked to that site),
      clicks what is needed (eg `1Y`) and reads the data the page loaded. For regular data it writes a
      parser, which the app checks (no imports, files, network or `eval`) and runs on the full data; small
      irregular data it copies. About 30 to 60 s and a few cents; at most 15 model requests.
    - A folded `from_url` row under the code says what was done (page text or browser, clicks, copied or
      parsed, rows, time, cost); unfold it for every browser step and every parser tried, with its result.
      The downloads and AI calls are in the debug log (`from_url`), the cost on the title bar's context meter.
    - What isn't on the page is `Not assigned: from_url didn't find it: <why>`; nothing is bound. Only
      public http(s) pages are read. Runs differ: the AI decides what to click, so check the row count.
  - **The AI**: one request, no tools; it reads the chat so far, your variables (and what `@` mentions hold)
    and the SmashDb tables. A proposal that isn't an assignment, or misses the name you gave, goes back to the
    model up to twice. Logged as `inline-assign` in the debug log, with its own card in the Agents tab; its
    cost is on the title bar's context meter.
- **`/script`: scripts the AI saves for itself** (`pkgs/ds/ai/scripts.py`; what must hold is in
  `spec/pkgs/ds/ai/scripts.md`). A `from_url` run that used the browser can be kept as a small Python file
  that gets the same data later with no AI (about 5 s, free, instead of 30 s and a few cents).
  - **Save**: after such a run its `from_url` row ends with "/script saves it as a script". `/script` (or
    `/script <name>`) has the AI write the file from what the run did (page, labels clicked, the data
    response, the parser); the draft is run with no AI and must give the same rows. It then shows as code
    in the `/assign` box: change it if you like, Enter saves `pkgs/ds/ai/temp/scripts/<id>.py` and rebuilds
    `registry.md` there. Esc drops it. Commit the files with git as any code.
  - **Use**: from then on `/assign` is told of the saved scripts and proposes `name = scripts.<id>(...)`
    when one fits, also with other arguments (another ticker, another range). The line under the code says
    "a saved script: no AI when run"; a `script` row under the result says what ran and how long it took.
  - **When one stops working** (it raises, its result doesn't fit its return type, or its own `_check`
    refuses it): the AI browser gets the value instead, the `script` row says why it failed, and `/script`
    then proposes the repaired file. Asked in a way a script doesn't cover yet, `/script` proposes adding a
    parameter to it rather than a second script.
  - **Always the file as it is now**: a run reads the file from disk, so your edits and the AI's apply on
    the next call. A file that breaks the script rules (one public function named as the file, typed,
    allowlisted imports, no global state) isn't run, and says which rule.
  - `/script list` lists them; `/script delete <id>` deletes one. Past 250,000 bytes of scripts, a save
    asks which to delete, least used first. Calls are logged to `local/ai_scripts/runs.jsonl`.
- **Keybindings**: Alt+K opens a searchable list of every shortcut, like Omarchy's SUPER+K: type to filter,
  Esc (or Alt+K) closes (`keys_palette`, `assets/keys.js`). Enter runs the picked shortcut, as in Omarchy,
  when a key press alone can run it (`commands.RUNNABLE`: the `Alt` keys; a ↵ marks those rows). Enter does
  nothing on keys that act on what you are typing (Enter in the chat, Tab in a cell).
- **Floating a view**: every view (a tab, a cell's result, a result unfolded in the chat) has a button at
  its top right that floats it over the page, nearly full screen; click it again, press Esc or click
  outside to put it back. It is the same component, only restyled in the browser (`.is-floating`,
  `assets/panes.js`), so its sort, filter and playing video carry on.
- **A second key** (`Binding.also`): a shortcut can have one more key for the same thing, matched wherever
  the first is and listed beside it (`Alt+\` / Alt+Enter`). Today the Terminal's two: `Alt+Enter` shows or
  hides it, as Omarchy's `SUPER+Enter` opens a terminal, and `Alt+Shift+Enter` is its full screen. Both work
  from anywhere, also from inside the shell and a Python cell.
- **Keyboard shortcuts** are all defined once, in `ui/shortcuts.py`, as the `Shortcut` enum named
  by what they do (`Shortcut.FULL_SCREEN`, `Shortcut.RUN`, …). The help panel, tooltips, the cell editor's
  keymap (`codemirror_keys`) and `assets/panes.js` (`window.SHORTCUTS`) all read it: change a key there only.
- **Panes**: each pane's title has an expand arrow (full screen) and a × that closes it (as its toggle; closing a
  full-screen pane goes back to the layout without it). The bottom bar toggles Chat (Alt+A, A for AI), Results (Alt+R), Python (Alt+J, J for Jupyter; Alt+P is the command palette), Variables (Alt+V) and the Terminal (``Alt+` ``, as VS Code's Ctrl+\`; an experiment), as in Zed. What every panel has is in `spec/services/ui/README.md` ("Panels"). Add Shift to make that pane full screen, from anywhere and even when it is hidden (`Alt+Shift+A` / `R` / `J` / `V`; the same key again restores the panes; `Alt+F` does it for the pane you are in). `Alt+W` closes every panel (as Omarchy's `SUPER+W` closes a window), so only the desktop's background shows. `Alt+Ctrl+J` works the Python and Variables panes as a pair: it shows both (so with one open it opens the other), and hides both only when both are open. (Neither letter follows
  Omarchy, where `SUPER+P` / `SUPER+J` are window layout actions with nothing comparable here.) Only the chat
  shows at first (results also unfold inline in it, and `open →` brings up Results); a pane
  whose neighbour is hidden takes the freed space. Hidden cells keep their text.
  Default widths with Results, Python and Variables all open: Variables is a narrow column (22% of the
  width, between 240 and 340 px: `--vars-width` in `assets/app.css`) and Results and Python share the rest,
  half each. Dragging Results' corner still resizes it.
- **Bars as Omarchy's**: the title bar and the bottom bar have the colour of Omarchy's own bar (`--bar` in
  `assets/app.css`: the theme's `background`, Everforest's `#2d353b`) and no dividing line, so they read as
  part of the desktop. The value is written in the CSS, not read from the theme: another Omarchy theme
  needs it changed there.
- **Desktop** (`ui/desktop.py`, `ui.desktop`): with every panel hidden (`State.no_panels`) the window shows
  the `background` setting's picture (see Config; by default this machine's wallpaper), as a desktop does, and nothing else: the keys that bring the panels back are
  the first section of the help panel (`?`, `Alt+H`). The default is Omarchy's `~/.local/state/omarchy/current/background`, a link it repoints to the
  current theme's background. The backend serves it at `GET /background`, read from disk on each request and
  sent with `Cache-Control: no-store` (no cache); the page asks for `/background?v=<the setting>`, so a new
  setting is fetched at once and a theme change shows on the next reload. A machine without the
  file gets a 404 and the plain dark background. Nothing shows behind an open panel.
- **Config: the app's settings** (`ui/config.py`, `services/ui/config.toml`): a `Config` class read from a
  TOML file in the repo, changed while the app runs. Today one setting, `background`.
  - **A setting is a private variable and a property**: `self.__background: Path | None = None` (None = not
    set) and `@property def background(self) -> Path`, which returns it or its default. The property's
    return type is the input's type and its docstring the help text. An optional `check_<name>(value)`
    refuses a value (`background`: the file must exist).
  - **Everything else is derived from the properties**, so a new setting is those lines and nothing more:
    `set_config(...)`'s parameters (its signature is built at import), `config.set_<name>(value)`, the
    file's keys, the Config widget's form and the Config tab.
  - **Changing one**: the **Config widget** (`/config`, `+` → Config, or `Edit` in the debug panel's Config
    tab) is a tool form on `set_config`, as VODs is on its tool: its inputs start as what is set now, an
    emptied input means "back to the default", Run applies it, and `Alt+I` has the AI fill the inputs (you
    run them). In a Python cell, `config` is predefined: `config.background`, `config.set_background("~/x.png")`.
    The chat agent has no tool for it.
  - **Hot reload**: a setting is read from the file each time it is used (no cache, no watcher), so a hand
    edit applies on the next request. A change made in the app is written to the file and the page's copy
    (`State.config`, re-read with the session) updates at once; what shows a setting references
    `State.config["<name>"]`.
  - **The file** holds only what is set (a missing key = the default); a path under `$HOME` is written with
    `~` so it works on every machine. A value that is refused changes nothing. A file that can't be read, a
    refused value in it or an unknown key leaves the defaults in use, and the Config tab says why.
  - **Debug panel → Config** (`Alt+D`): every setting with its value in use, `set` or `default`, type and
    what it is. Read-only; `Edit` opens the widget.
- **Variables** (`Alt+V`, the bottom bar's fourth toggle; `ui/variables.py`; what must hold is in
  `spec/services/ui/variables.md`): a pane at the right of Results / Python listing the
  session's Python names that are data: the agent's results (`r1`, …), a SmashDb console's saves (`q1`, …),
  cell results opened as tabs (`out3`) and whatever your cells assign. Each row has its type, shape, rough
  size and where it came from (the tool, `SmashDb console`, `cell [3]`, `python`). Modules, functions and
  classes are left out unless `All` (in the panel's head) is on; `pl`, `db` and `_names` never show.
  - Click a name to open its Results tab (again, if you closed it); a value with no view unfolds its details
    instead. `▸` unfolds the details of any row: the tool inputs that made it, other names bound to the same
    object, a table's columns and types, or the value's repr.
  - **The head is one line**, also in the narrow column it is beside Results and Python: the name, a summary
    (cut with an ellipsis when there is no room), `All`, `Clear` and the full screen arrows.
  - **Clearing**: the `×` on a row, or `Clear` for the ticked rows (row checkboxes; the header's checkbox
    ticks all or none; the head then says what the ticked rows hold together, eg `selected 2 · 81 KB`, and
    the button `Clear (2)`). It removes the names from Python, as `del` would: `r1` is a `NameError`, its tab
    closes. There is one `Clear`, no `Clear all` button: everything at once is the header checkbox then
    `Clear`, `/clear-variables`, or the palette's `Variables: Clear all` (which also has
    `Variables: Undo the last clear`).
  - **Undo, then really gone**: after a clear the pane's bottom line says what was cleared, with an `Undo`
    button whose bottom edge is a bar that runs down over 3 seconds (`variables.UNDO_SECONDS`). `Undo`
    puts the batch back; a name you bound again in that time is left as it is and named. When the bar is
    empty (or on the `×` beside it, "free now", or at the next clear) the batch is dropped for good with
    everything else in the app that held those objects (`_`, a cell result showing one, a tool form's
    record of it), the garbage collector runs, and the line says what was freed. A clear run from the
    palette while the pane is hidden shows the pane, so its Undo is on screen.
    `Session.clear` / `restore` / `purge` do this; the held batch is the original objects waiting to be
    dropped, not a cache (nothing is read from it but Undo). The bar is drawn by the browser from the
    moment the line appears; the server's own 3 s timer is what frees.
  - What clearing can't free: an object still bound to another name (`a = r1`; the details say so), and an
    agent result that is a model (VODs, player usage), which is also part of the chat history the
    agent needs. Tables aren't affected: the DataFrame is its own object, apart from the chat's CSV text.
  - `r` numbers are never given out again after a clear, so "r2" in the chat can't come to mean another
    table. `q` names are (a console suggests the first free one).
  - The pane is only kept current while it is on screen. `Alt+V` isn't Omarchy's `SUPER+V` (universal
    paste): Omarchy has no matching action, so it is `Alt` + a free letter, V for variables.
- **Full screen**: each pane has a button with two diagonal arrows (top right) that fills the window
  with that pane; click it again to restore. Alt+F (`Shortcut.FULL_SCREEN`) floats the view you are in
  (see Floating a view), or, outside a view, fills the window with your pane: "you are in" is where
  keyboard focus is, else what you last clicked (`assets/panes.js`). The bottom-bar toggles
  keep their state while a pane is full screen; clicking one leaves full screen and shows that pane.
- **VODs** (match videos): one component, the list plus the video picked from it. Click a card to play it:
  the list folds away so the video fills the component, and "Show list" in the player's bar brings it
  back under the player. It works the same in a tab and in a cell's result, each with its own picked
  video. Leaving a tab stops its video; it is back, paused, when you return. Prev / Next fetch the search's other
  pages. Videos whose uploader disabled embedding show YouTube's own message; use the "Open ↗" button.
  The player is the Browser widget's frame (`render.web_frame`) with the list's own button added.
- **A panel's `?`** (`ui.keys_button`; today the Python console and the Terminal): opens the keybindings list
  (`Alt+K`) with its search box already holding that panel's word (`cell`, `terminal`), so only its keys show.
  The picture in the title bar's left corner is a button too: a click opens the command palette (`Alt+P`).
- **Terminal** (EXPERIMENT, branch `exp/ghostty-terminal`; a **panel**, ``Alt+` ``, full screen ``Alt+Shift+` ``; `ui/terminal.py`):
  a shell on this machine in [ghostty-web](https://github.com/coder/ghostty-web) (Ghostty's terminal in the
  browser, 0.4.0 from jsdelivr), in a strip under the bottom row as VS Code's (alone, it takes the height under
  the chat). The panel frames the backend's `GET /terminal` page, which talks to `/terminal/ws`: `$SHELL -l` in
  a pseudo-terminal, started through util-linux's `setsid --ctty` (no fork of the threaded server). Only this
  machine's pages may connect (localhost client and origin). One shell, started the first time the panel shows
  and kept while it is hidden; a page reload starts a new one. When the shell ends (`exit`, or a backend
  restart: every code change while developing) the page says so at the bottom right, and Enter starts a new one.
  - **Inline chat (`Alt+I` in the Terminal; `ui/inline_terminal.py`)**: the same inline AI as a cell's, for
    the shell. A box over the bottom lines; Enter sends what you typed and the text of the visible screen to
    `POST /inline_terminal` (agent `inline-terminal`: no tools, one request, knowing the chat so far and adding
    nothing to it). The command is pasted at the prompt and **never run**: you press Enter. Nothing is typed,
    and the box says why, when the ask was not for a command (the AI's short answer shows in the box), the
    command has several lines, the call failed, or a full-screen program (vim, less) has the terminal. Esc
    closes the box. Each call is an "agent" record in the debug log (origin "inline terminal") and is added to
    the session's cost and to Spend, as the other inline chats. Only this machine's pages may call the route.
    `Alt+I` again closes the box, in a cell too (as Esc: a proposal is discarded, a late answer is dropped).
    The box is the one a cell's inline chat shows (`ui/inline_box.js`: the robot, the input, the status text
    and its look, in one file); the Terminal's page gets it from the backend (`GET /inline_box.js`).
- **Browser** (kind `browser`, `ui/web.py`; `+` → Browser): a web page in a frame, under an address box
  (Enter loads what you type; `https://` is added when missing), `Alt+← Back · Alt+→ Forward` (the browser's own keys:
  they step through pages followed by clicking inside the page) and "Open ↗" (a real browser tab). A link
  clicked in a widget (`render.link`) or in the AI's answer opens here, **as a glance** (as in Zen): the one
  `web` tab's Browser floats over the app; Esc or a click outside closes it and puts the layout back as it
  was, its float button (or Alt+F) docks it into Results as the `web` tab. The next link loads into the same
  tab. Ctrl / Shift / middle click still opens a real browser tab. Some links are rewritten to a form a frame
  can show (`web.EMBED_RULES`, eg a YouTube watch link to its embed player). Many sites (GitHub, SmashWiki,
  start.gg, X) refuse to be framed (`X-Frame-Options` / CSP `frame-ancestors`, against clickjacking), which
  the page itself can't detect. So a clicked link's site is checked first (`web.frameable`, `GET /frameable`:
  one logged HEAD request, given up after 0.5 s, not cached): a site that refuses opens in a real browser
  tab instead; a slow or failed check opens the glance anyway, and the hint under it says to use Open ↗.
  An address typed in the Browser is checked the same way: a refusing site shows a card in the frame's place
  (`github.com can't be shown here (x-frame-options: deny)` and a big "Open in new tab ↗"), not a blank
  frame. The hint only shows when the check had no answer. GitHub can take ~0.6 s the first time a page is
  asked for (then ~60 ms), so a first check may miss the 0.5 s limit and fall back to the hint.
- **Python cells**: Jupyter-style, each a CodeMirror editor with Everforest syntax colors.
  Shift+Enter runs a cell and moves to the next (adding one after the last), Ctrl+Enter runs in
  place, Tab indents. **The console has no buttons of its own: it is worked from the keyboard**, from the
  cell the cursor is in (the keys are `Shortcut.RUN_ALL` ... `CELL_DOWN` in `shortcuts.py`, handled by
  `cell_editor.jsx`): `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` runs all cells (this cell as typed), `Alt+Z` clears every output,
  `Alt+N` adds a cell under this one and goes to it (it was `Alt+Enter` until that became the Terminal's second key), `Alt+Backspace` deletes this cell (the cursor goes to
  the one above; not while cells run; no undo), `Alt+ArrowUp` / `Alt+ArrowDown` go to the cell above / below
  (these two replace CodeMirror's "move line up / down"). The title line names the main ones; hover it for
  all. Each cell keeps its own ▶ and × (and the bug, on hover). With the cursor in no cell, the command palette
  has `Python: Run all cells`, `Clear outputs` and `New cell` (which adds at the end). `pl` (polars) and `db` (`ds.data.SmashDb`) are predefined. A cell ending in a
  DataFrame (polars or pandas, or a Series) shows it in a compact version of the tables-pane grid (8 rows visible, columns sized
  to content, each header showing its polars dtype in italics on a second line, like polars' own notebook
  view; click a header to sort);
  "Open as tab" moves it up there as `out<n>`. Any value with a view (see Rendering) that you bind to a name becomes a tab. Variables persist until the server restarts.
- **Completion**: pops up as you type. Tab accepts the highlighted suggestion (Enter also works), or
  opens the list after a name or a dot; elsewhere Tab indents. Ctrl+Space forces the list. Suggestions come from `jedi` run
  against the live variables, so `r1.` lists real DataFrame methods. `jedi` is present in the root
  venv only as a dependency of IPython; add it to the root `pyproject.toml` if that changes.
- **Inline chat** (as Copilot's Ctrl+I; `ui/inline_edit.jsx` + `inline_edit.py`): in a Python
  cell or a SmashDb console's SQL box, `Alt+I` opens a prompt box under the editor. The AI also reads the
  chat so far (its answers and tool results), so "a query for the move we just talked about" works; slower
  and costlier the longer the chat is. (A second key that left the chat out was dropped, Nov 2026.)

  Type what you want and press Enter: the AI rewrites the selection (or the whole box when nothing is
  selected) and the change is shown as a diff in the editor. Tab accepts (one Ctrl+Z undoes it), Esc
  discards, Enter with a new prompt refines the proposal. While the AI is thinking, light sweeps
  across the lines it is rewriting. Either way the model sees the editor's text
  plus the SmashDb tables (columns, their first rows, and notes on how values are written: a move is
  `Neutral Air`, not `nair`; a startup is text like `10/13/16`) and, for Python, your live variables
  (DataFrames with their columns and first rows). A proposal for the whole box is checked before you see
  it: a query is run, Python is parsed; one that fails (or a query that returns no rows) goes back to the
  model with the error, up to twice. It only reads the chat: an inline call is not added to it, and it has
  none of the chat agent's tools. Each call is one record in the debug log, with the same usage as a chat
  turn (tokens, cost, `model requests`), and the box's status line ends with what the call used
  (`$0.0004 · 9.2k in · 120 out · 1 request`). Its cost is added to the title bar's context meter; the meter's size
  stays the chat's, since the call isn't added to the chat. Another editor gets it by
  passing `edit_url` (`editor.py`).
- **Inline chat in a widget** (`ui/inline_fill.py`; what must hold is in
  `spec/services/ui/inline_ai.md`): a widget with a tool form works like a function, inputs in
  and a result out, so there the same `Alt+I` (or the robot button next to `Inputs`) asks the AI for the
  **inputs**. The form unfolds with an Ask AI row on top: type `sparg0 vs steve, offline, last 90 sets`, Enter.
  The form then shows the AI's inputs, the changed ones outlined (hover one for its old value), and a line with
  what the call used (`2 changed · $0.0003 · 2.4k in · 40 out · 1 request`).
  - **The AI never runs the tool; you do.** The box takes the focus back after a proposal, so Enter again (the
    box empty) or Run runs it. Text in the box means "ask", so a new instruction refines the proposal.
  - Esc, the row's × or the robot button closes the row, and the inputs go back to the ones that made the result.
  - The AI changes what is on screen: inputs you typed but didn't run are sent along, as is the last proposal.
  - Its answer is the tool's own parameter schema (`ToolForm.fill_schema`, without hidden parameters such as
    `page`) and must pass the tool's own validator (`ToolForm.check`); a refused answer goes back to the model
    with the validator's words, up to twice, then the row shows the error and the form stays as it was.
  - It reads the chat so far and has no tools, so it can't look anything up (eg which of two players sharing a
    tag you mean); what the tool itself refuses (an unknown player) only shows when you run.
  - Generic: nothing is written per widget. A widget gets it by having a `tool` in `widgets.py`. Today that is
    VODs and Player usage; a not-yet-run form (`+`) works too.
  - Logged and counted like the editor's inline chat: one `inline-fill` record in the debug log (its `↖` goes
    to the result), its cost on the title bar's context meter, its own row in the debug panel's Agents and Spend tabs.
  - Inside the SmashDb console's SQL box, `Alt+I` is still the code inline chat.
  - Not covered: the things a view changes without its tool (a table's filter, sort and `SQL ▸`, the usage
    view's window, the videos page), and table results (head to head, tournaments, frame data), which have no
    tool form yet (the spec says why).
- **No autofill**: every input, textarea and editor is opted out of password managers (1Password, LastPass,
  Bitwarden, Dashlane) and browser autofill by `assets/no_autofill.js`, including inputs added later. To allow
  one, put `data-allow-autofill` on it or a parent.
- **Local only**: the backend binds to 127.0.0.1, since the app executes arbitrary Python.

Layout: `ui/session.py` (namespace, agent, completion; no UI), `render.py` (Python value -> view -> component), `state.py` (Reflex
state), `ui.py` (components), `editor.py` + `cell_editor.jsx` (CodeMirror wrapper),
`api.py` (`POST /complete`), `logs.py` / `spend.py` / `agents.py` / `perf.py` (the debug panel's tabs), `assets/app.css` (Everforest). Design mockups this came from:
`experimental/design_poc` (`/split`).
